name: shipyard2-neural-retrieval
title: 209 sessions: neural embeddings and other tools at finding the session
command: bench/shipyard2/results/README.md for the two tools; hosted models: each window of what people and agents wrote embedded through a hosted API, exact scan, first five distinct sessions

conditions.corpus: the second shipyard corpus, 209 sessions and 139 questions, none used for tuning
conditions.tools: cass 0.11.0 with its MiniLM model and episodic-memory 1.6.0, each run in a container with no network during queries
conditions.hosted models: windows of 1,200 characters of what people and agents wrote, tool output left out, embedded through OpenRouter; only this public corpus was sent
conditions.scoring: every session holding the answer among the first five returned; no model judges anything

summary: A small static embedding model added nothing at this size. This asks the same of real neural models: the two session-search tools that use one, and ten hosted models scanned exactly with no keyword search at all.
baseline: ctx's keyword search: 125 of 139 in the session's own terms, 23 paraphrased
bar: a difference counts only if a sign test on the paired questions gives p below 0.05 (set in bench/head-to-head.md)
meaning: For one search on a reworded question, neural embeddings are far better than keywords, and the model is what decides by how much. Small models from 2019 to 2022, which the other tools use, find 37 to 55 of the 139 paraphrased questions; current models find 62 to 87; ctx's keywords find 23. In the session's own terms the best models also edge ahead, 134 against 125. What unit of text is embedded matters little. Blending a strong model's ranking with the keyword ranking at equal weight throws away most of its gain on paraphrased questions. None of this is in ctx: whether it changes what an agent answers is the next result.
